I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

I can't rely on other people
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette:
Daniel Ortega was 32, single, and worked as a park ranger in a wide state park outside a North American city, a job that had once fit him so naturally that he had thought of it less as work than as a way of life. Before the trauma, he liked the quiet routines of the ranger station, the long drives between trailheads, and the way visitors stopped him for directions with an easy trust he had never questioned. That trust changed after he was abducted while off duty, held for hours, and tortured in a setting he still struggled to describe in any coherent way. When he tried to tell the story in intake, Daniel would begin with the same few details-being taken, the sense of not knowing where he was, the fact that there were moments he could still see with terrible clarity-and then his voice would flatten and the thread would break. He would stop, stare down at his hands, and say that the rest was "gone" or "just not in words." Some parts of the event stayed sharply preserved in his mind, especially the moments that came with particular physical sensations or visual fragments, but other stretches were blank to him, as if they belonged to someone else's life. That unevenness frightened him almost as much as the event itself. He had come to believe that if his own memory could split apart like that, then something in him must have been permanently damaged.

In the months that followed, Daniel began to move through his days as if always preparing for a challenge he could not name. Before nearly any interaction he rehearsed what he would say, sometimes under his breath and sometimes silently while standing in the hallway outside the ranger office. He would prepare questions, greetings, and explanations in advance, because in the moment he often felt unable to trust his own words to come out in the right order. At work, this showed up most when a visitor approached unexpectedly or a coworker asked him something simple and he needed a second to think; he became visibly tense, as though he had already been caught off guard. He also started numbing his feelings rather than letting himself register what came up. In the evenings he could sit alone in his apartment for long stretches, detached and muted, going through the motions of eating or cleaning up without much sense of being emotionally present. He did not describe this as calm so much as deliberate shutting down, a way of keeping anything from reaching him too directly.

Certain ordinary delays became especially difficult. If a hiker was late returning from a trail, if a supervisor took longer than expected to answer a radio call, if a vehicle did not arrive when it should, Daniel's mind jumped immediately to the worst possibility. He would feel certain that something bad was happening, even when there was no evidence beyond the passing of a few extra minutes. In the park, where waiting for updates and watching for visitors was part of the job, this meant he often spent those intervals on edge, scanning for signs that danger was already underway. His body seemed to react before his mind could fully catch up. He described it as a jolt that happened first in his chest and muscles, a surge of alarm that arrived before he had a thought to attach to it. That physical response made him feel unreliable in his own skin, and he became increasingly wary of situations that might set it off.

Driving became one of the clearest ways his life narrowed. Daniel avoided driving whenever he could and felt tense even as a passenger in a vehicle. The ranger truck, which had once been a practical extension of his work, now carried the sense of confinement and helplessness. He found excuses to trade routes with other staff or to walk when he could, and over time that avoidance affected how he moved through both his job and his personal life. It made him dependent on others in ways that embarrassed him, though the embarrassment was mixed with something more basic: he did not believe he could trust anyone else to keep him safe. That belief had grown alongside his experience of being unable to rely on others during the trauma itself, and it now colored how he interpreted ordinary human limits. Even in the station, where colleagues checked in on him kindly, he watched himself for any sign that he might need help and then hesitated to ask for it.

Daniel's fear that he was "going crazy" was tied to these experiences. The intensity of his reactions, the blank stretches in his memory, and the strange feeling that his body knew danger before his mind did made him worry that he was losing control of himself. He recognized that these fears had become part of daily life when he found himself repeatedly checking doors and windows at home, then checking them again, sometimes more than once before bed or before leaving for work. He would stand at the apartment door with his keys in hand, then turn back to test the locks one more time, unable to shake the feeling that something was not secure. Coming to treatment was not easy for him; it took the accumulation of missed turns on familiar roads, strained moments with coworkers, and the growing exhaustion of living so narrowly. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep explaining away the changes. He was hoping for a way to understand what had happened to him without losing the thread, and he was most afraid that the damage he felt in his body and mind would leave him permanently unable to trust anyone, including himself.
